options: A single Axes object
A Figure and an array of two Axes
Two separate Figures
A DataFrame of two columns
questions.explain: plt.subplots(nrows, ncols) returns a Figure and an array (or single object when 1x1) of Axes; with one row and two columns you index axes[0] and axes[1].

questions.q: Why use sharey=True when plotting two comparable charts side by side?
options: It makes the charts render faster
It uses the same y-scale in both panels, so bar heights can be compared honestly
It automatically colors both charts identically
It saves the figure to a file
questions.explain: Shared axes give the panels the same scale, so differences in height reflect real differences in data rather than different axis ranges.

questions.q: In fig.add_gridspec(2, 3), what does fig.add_subplot(gs[0, :]) create?
options: An axes in the bottom-right cell only
A 2 by 3 grid of separate axes
An axes spanning every column of the top row
A copy of the previous axes
questions.explain: gs[0, :] means row 0 and all columns, so the axes stretches across the full top row, ideal for a wide trend chart.

questions.q: In Plotly, how do you place a bar chart in the left panel of a 1x2 subplot figure?
options: fig.add_trace(go.Bar(...)) then call fig.left()
Pass sharey=True to go.Bar
Call plt.subplots(1, 2) first
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(...), row=1, col=1) on a figure made with make_subplots
questions.explain: make_subplots creates the grid, and each trace is added with row and col arguments that choose its panel.

questions.q: Which is a sound dashboard principle from this lesson?
options: Give each panel one clear question and keep colors and scales consistent
Fit as many charts as possible onto one page
Use a different color scheme for every panel
Put the least important chart top-left
questions.explain: Effective dashboards give each panel one question, place the key chart top-left, stay consistent in style and stop at around six panels.
